title: Core learning techniques
introHtml:
The two techniques with the strongest evidence are practice testing and spaced practice. The rest work best as add-ons to them.

TechniqueWhat you doEvidenceBest forTime per paragraph
Active recall (practice testing)Close the source and answer questions, write what you remember, or explain it aloud. Then check.StrongEverything. It should be the core of every study session.~30 s per question (1×)
Spaced repetitionReview the same material at growing intervals (for example 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days). Apps like Anki schedule it for you.StrongHigh-volume facts and anything needed months later: vocabulary, formulas, dates, case names, anatomy.~2-3 min in total over a month (~4-6×)
Blank-page recall (brain dump)After a lecture or chapter, write or sketch everything you remember on a blank page, then fill the gaps from the source in another colour.Strong (a form of retrieval)Same-day review of lectures and chapters in any subject; finding gaps fast.~2 min (~4×)
Practice questionsExam-style questions, then study the explanation for every wrong or guessed answer.StrongApplying knowledge: maths and physics problems, essay plans, legal problem questions, code exercises, clinical cases; exam preparation; finding weak topics.~2-3 min per question (~4-6×)
InterleavingMix related topics or problem types in one session instead of blocking one topic at a time.Moderate to strongTopics that are easy to confuse: verb tenses, integration methods, painters' styles, similar diseases or drug classes.~0 extra; it reorders the work (~1×)
Elaborative interrogationFor each fact, ask "why is this true?" and "what happens if it fails?", and answer from your own knowledge.ModerateTurning isolated facts into connected understanding: history, biology, economics, law.~3-5 min (~6-10×)
Self-explanationWhile studying an example or a figure, explain each step to yourself and how it links to what you know.ModerateMechanisms, worked examples, proofs, code, pathways.~3-5 min (~6-10×)
Feynman technique (teach it)Explain a topic in plain words as if to a 12-year-old. Where you get stuck or use jargon you can't unpack is where your understanding stops.ModerateCore concepts in any field: physics, economics, physiology, statistics.~8-15 min (~15-30×)
Learning by teachingTeach a classmate, a study group, or even an empty room. Preparing to teach also helps.ModerateConsolidating a topic you already studied.~20-40 min incl. preparation (~40-80×)
Dual codingPair words with visuals: diagrams, flowcharts, timelines, sketches. Redraw them from memory.ModerateProcesses, structures and sequences: anatomy, historical timelines, circuits, chemical cycles, algorithms.~5-10 min (~10-20×)
Concrete examplesLink every abstract idea to a concrete case or example.ModerateAbstract principles: economics models, legal doctrines, maths definitions, pharmacology.~3-5 min for two examples (~6-10×)
PretestingTry questions on a topic before you study it. Getting them wrong primes you to notice the answers.ModerateBefore a lecture or a new chapter.~1-2 min for 2-3 questions (~2-4×)
Successive relearningKeep retrieving each item until you get it right, then come back on later days and do it again.StrongCombining recall and spacing into one routine.~3-4 min in total, spread out (~6-8×)

How to read the time column. The unit is one recall question about a dense ~150-word paragraph you have already read once: about 30 seconds, counted as 1×. The other figures are rough estimates from typical practice, not measured values. The point is the comparison: cheap techniques (recall questions, flashcards) give the most retention per minute and should be your daily base; expensive ones (teaching, concept maps, summaries) buy deeper understanding and are worth it for the 10-20% of ideas that everything else hangs on.

items.title: Active recall (practice testing)
items.leadHtml: Close the source and answer questions, write what you remember, or explain it aloud. Then check. It works for every subject and should be the core of every study session.

parts.why: A memory is less like a file in a cabinet and more like a path through a field: every time you walk it, it gets easier to find. Re-reading shows you the path from above; recall makes you walk it. Pulling something out of memory changes the memory itself, strengthening it and adding new routes to it. It also gives you honest feedback. Re-reading makes everything feel familiar, but only a closed-book attempt tells you whether you can produce the answer when it counts.
parts.how:
1. Read or listen to a section once, with full attention.
  2. Close the book or hide the notes.
  3. Answer questions about it (your own, the textbook's, or the learning objectives turned into questions), out loud or on paper.
  4. Check against the source and mark what you missed or got wrong.
  5. Come back to the misses later, not straight away (see spaced repetition).

examples.simple: After a Spanish lesson, cover the English column of your vocabulary list and say each Spanish word's meaning before checking.
examples.nontrivial: A history student reads about the causes of the First World War, then asks herself "What would have happened if Britain had stayed neutral?" She cannot answer from the text directly, so she has to retrieve several facts and combine them. Recall that forces you to use knowledge, not just repeat it, is the strongest version, and it also shows which links between facts are missing.
examples.html:
• Simple: After a Spanish lesson, cover the English column of your vocabulary list and say each Spanish word's meaning before checking.
  • Non-trivial: A history student reads about the causes of the First World War, then asks herself "What would have happened if Britain had stayed neutral?" She cannot answer from the text directly, so she has to retrieve several facts and combine them. Recall that forces you to use knowledge, not just repeat it, is the strongest version, and it also shows which links between facts are missing.

parts.time: About 30 seconds per question (1×, the baseline). Three questions on a paragraph take about the same time as re-reading it twice, and leave far more behind.
parts.watch:
• Checking too early. Peeking after two seconds turns recall back into re-reading. Give each question a real attempt first.
  • Asking only "what" questions. Mix in "why", "how" and "what if" so you test understanding, not just labels.
  • Mistaking difficulty for failure. Struggling to recall is the workout, not a sign that the method isn't working.

reading.html: Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science.

items.title: Spaced repetition
items.leadHtml: Review the same material at growing intervals (for example 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days). Apps like Anki schedule it for you. It suits high-volume facts and anything you need months later.

parts.why: Each time you recall something, its forgetting slows down, so the next review can wait longer. The key is timing. Retrieving a memory that is half-forgotten is the workout: the effort of finding it is what makes it stronger. Retrieving one you saw ten minutes ago is a stroll, pleasant but with little training effect. Spacing deliberately lets a bit of forgetting happen so that each review counts. Massed study (the same thing many times in one evening) feels productive because the material is still fresh, which is exactly why it builds less.
parts.how:
1. Learn the material once and make a few recall prompts (cards or questions).
  2. Review after about a day, then after about 3 days, a week, two weeks and a month.
  3. If you fail an item, shorten its next gap; if it was easy, lengthen it.
  4. Let an app (Anki, or the flashcard tool you prefer) do the scheduling for large volumes. For whole topics, put review dates in your calendar.
  5. Do the reviews due today before learning anything new.

examples.simple: A music student learning the key signatures reviews them on the bus on days 1, 3, 7 and 14, and by the end of the month names any key instantly.
examples.nontrivial: A law student has an exam in eight weeks and a second one, built on the first, in a year. For the near exam, gaps of a few days to a week are best. For the material she needs in a year, she stretches later reviews to a month or more. Research suggests the best gap grows with how long you need to remember: roughly 10-20% of the time until the test for delays of weeks, and a smaller share (around 5-10%) when the test is a year away.
examples.html:
• Simple: A music student learning the key signatures reviews them on the bus on days 1, 3, 7 and 14, and by the end of the month names any key instantly.
  • Non-trivial: A law student has an exam in eight weeks and a second one, built on the first, in a year. For the near exam, gaps of a few days to a week are best. parts.time: About 5 short reviews of a paragraph over a month take ~2-3 minutes in total, spread out (~4-6×). That is less than re-reading it twice a week, and it keeps the material for months rather than days.
parts.watch:
• Letting reviews pile up. A missed week becomes hundreds of due cards. Short daily sessions beat a weekly marathon.
  • Spacing without recall. Re-reading on day 7 is spaced, but it is not practice. Each review should be a closed-book attempt.
  • Cards without understanding. Spacing keeps what you learned; it does not make sense of it. Understand first, then space.

items.title: Blank-page recall (brain dump)
items.leadHtml: After a lecture or chapter, write or sketch everything you remember on a blank page, then fill the gaps from the source in another colour. It is a form of retrieval, ideal for same-day review and for finding gaps fast.

parts.why: A question gives you a cue; a blank page gives you none. You have to rebuild the structure of the topic yourself: what came first, what depends on what, what belongs together. That is the same organising work an exam essay or a real problem asks for. The second colour then makes your gaps visible at a glance, so you know exactly what to study next instead of re-reading everything.
parts.how:
1. Close everything. Take a blank sheet and write the topic at the top.
  2. For 5-10 minutes, write or sketch all you remember: key points, links, diagrams, examples. Don't worry about order or neatness.
  3. When you run dry, wait a minute. More usually comes.
  4. Open the source and add what you missed or got wrong in a different colour.
  5. The coloured parts are tomorrow's recall questions.

examples.simple: After a biology lecture on the cell cycle, a student sketches the phases from memory and notices in red that she forgot what happens at the checkpoints.
examples.nontrivial: A programmer learning a new web framework does a brain dump of "what happens between a request arriving and a page being sent back". His sketch has the right parts but in the wrong order, and the middleware step is missing. No single flashcard would have shown that, because each part on its own was "known". Blank-page recall tests the connections, not just the pieces.
examples.html:
• Simple: After a biology lecture on the cell cycle, a student sketches the phases from memory and notices in red that she forgot what happens at the checkpoints.
  • Non-trivial: A programmer learning a new web framework does a brain dump of "what happens between a request arriving and a page being sent back". His sketch has the right parts but in the wrong order, and the middleware step is missing. No single flashcard would have shown that, because each part on its own was "known". Blank-page recall tests the connections, not just the pieces.

parts.time: About 2 minutes for one paragraph (~4×). For a whole lecture, 10-20 minutes plus the time to fill gaps.
parts.watch:
• Doing it with notes in view. Even glancing turns it into copying.
  • Filling gaps silently and moving on. The coloured items need to come back in later reviews, or the same gaps will reappear.
  • Expecting it to be tidy. A messy page full of red is a successful session.

items.title: Practice questions
items.leadHtml: Exam-style questions, then study the explanation for every wrong or guessed answer. They are best for applying knowledge, preparing for exams and finding weak topics.

parts.why: Knowing a fact and using it are different skills. A practice question makes you recognise which knowledge a situation calls for and apply it under constraints, which is what exams and real work ask. Wrong answers are the most valuable part. A mistake you made, followed quickly by the correct answer and the reason, is remembered better than a fact you simply read, because the error marks the exact spot where your understanding broke.
parts.how:
1. Use past papers, question banks, end-of-chapter problems, or questions you write from learning objectives.
  2. Answer without notes, and commit to an answer before checking.
  3. Mark each one: right and sure, right but guessed, or wrong.
  4. For every guessed or wrong answer, read the explanation and write one line on why the right answer is right and why yours wasn't.
  5. Keep an error log and redo those questions a few days later.

examples.simple: A physics student does five problems on Newton's second law and gets one wrong because she forgot to include friction. That single error teaches her more than the four she got right.
examples.nontrivial: An economics student notices that most of her errors are on questions where she picks an answer that is true but doesn't answer what was asked. Her error log shows the problem is reading, not knowledge. Sorting mistakes by type (didn't know, misread, confused two ideas, ran out of time) tells you whether to study content, slow down, or practise timing.
examples.html:
• Simple: A physics student does five problems on Newton's second law and gets one wrong because she forgot to include friction. That single error teaches her more than the four she got right.
  • Non-trivial: An economics student notices that most of her errors are on questions where she picks an answer that is true but doesn't answer what was asked. Her error log shows the problem is reading, not knowledge. Sorting mistakes by type (didn't know, misread, confused two ideas, ran out of time) tells you whether to study content, slow down, or practise timing.

parts.time: About 2-3 minutes per exam-style question, including reading the explanation (~4-6×). More than a simple recall question, because it also trains application and exam technique.
parts.watch:
• Saving questions for the last two weeks. Start early; they are a learning tool, not only a test.
  • Chasing scores. Doing the same bank twice may raise the percentage through memory of the answers, not understanding.
  • Skipping explanations for correct guesses. A lucky guess is a gap that hasn't shown itself yet.

items.title: Interleaving
items.leadHtml: Mix related topics or problem types in one session instead of blocking one topic at a time. It works best for topics that are easy to confuse.

parts.why: When you practise in blocks (ten problems on the same method), the heading at the top of the page has already told you which method to use. You skip the hardest step of a real problem: deciding which strategy applies. Interleaving puts that decision back in. Each problem asks "what kind of problem is this?" before "how do I solve it?". It also places similar things side by side, so you notice the differences between them, which is exactly what you need when two ideas look alike. It feels slower and less fluent, and that is the point.
parts.how:
1. Learn each topic or method on its own first, so you have something to mix.
  2. Build practice sets that mix 3-4 related types, in an unpredictable order.
  3. Before solving each item, name its type ("this is integration by parts because…").
  4. Prefer mixing things that are easy to confuse. Mixing unrelated subjects (French and chemistry) helps much less.

examples.simple: A French learner practises the passé composé and the imparfait in one mixed set of sentences instead of one tense per day, and has to decide each time which one fits.
examples.nontrivial: An art history student studies paintings by six similar artists. Seeing one painting from each artist in turn, rather than all paintings by one artist and then the next, helps her identify new paintings later, even though she feels she learned better from the blocks. Your sense of how well a method worked is not a reliable judge here: blocking feels better and works worse.

  • Non-trivial: An art history student studies paintings by six similar artists. parts.watch:
• Interleaving too early. If you can't yet do each type alone, mixing only causes confusion.
  • Mixing unrelated topics. The benefit comes from having to discriminate between similar things.
  • Giving up because scores dip. Performance during practice is lower; performance on the test later is higher.

items.title: Elaborative interrogation
items.leadHtml: For each fact, ask "why is this true?" and "what happens if it fails?", and answer from your own knowledge. It turns isolated facts into connected understanding.

parts.why: An isolated fact has one thread holding it in memory; a fact you have explained is tied to everything you used to explain it. Asking "why?" forces you to connect the new fact to what you already know, and those connections become extra routes back to it later. It also exposes facts you have accepted without understanding. If you can't answer "why?", you have found a gap before the exam does.
parts.how:
1. Take one fact or claim from your notes.
  2. Ask "why is this true?", "why here and not elsewhere?" or "what would happen if it were different?".
  3. Answer in a sentence or two from your own knowledge, before looking anything up.
  4. Check your answer against the source and fix it if needed.
  5. Keep the best "why" questions as recall questions for later.

examples.simple: "Water expands when it freezes." Why? Because the molecules lock into a hexagonal lattice that holds them further apart than in the liquid. What follows? Ice floats, so lakes freeze from the top and fish survive the winter.
examples.nontrivial: A history student reads "the printing press helped the Reformation spread". Asking "why the printing press, and why then?" leads her to cheap pamphlets, rising literacy in towns, and the fact that Luther wrote in German, not Latin. One fact becomes a small causal network she can use in an essay. The richer your prior knowledge, the better the answers, so this technique grows more powerful as you go deeper into a subject.

items.bodyHtml:
For each fact, ask "why is this true?" and "what happens if it fails?", and answer from your own knowledge. It turns isolated facts into connected understanding.

If you can't answer "why?", you have found a gap before the exam does.

How to do it.

  1. Take one fact or claim from your notes.
  2. Ask "why is this true?", "why here and not elsewhere?" or "what would happen if it were different?".
  3. Answer in a sentence or two from your own knowledge, before looking anything up.
  4. Check your answer against the source and fix it if needed.
  5. Keep the best "why" questions as recall questions for later.

Examples.

  • Simple: "Water expands when it freezes." Why? Because the molecules lock into a hexagonal lattice that holds them further apart than in the liquid. What follows? Ice floats, so lakes freeze from the top and fish survive the winter.

items.title: Self-explanation
items.leadHtml: While studying an example or a figure, explain each step to yourself and how it links to what you know. It suits mechanisms, worked examples, proofs, code and pathways.

parts.why: Reading a worked solution is like watching someone drive: everything looks obvious until you take the wheel. 1. Take a worked example, a proof, a diagram or a piece of code.
  2. Go one step or line at a time. Before moving on, say or write: what this step does, why it is needed, and how it follows from the one before.
  3. Link it to a rule or principle you already know ("this is the chain rule again").
  4. When you can't explain a step, mark it and resolve it from the source or by asking.
  5. Afterwards, try a similar problem without the example.

examples.nontrivial: A programming student reads a short sorting function and explains each line aloud. • Paraphrasing instead of explaining. "Then they add 3" describes; "they add 3 to both sides to keep the equation balanced" explains.

items.title: Feynman technique (explain it simply)
items.leadHtml: Explain a topic in plain words as if to a 12-year-old. Where you get stuck or use jargon you can't unpack is where your understanding stops.

parts.why: Most of us feel we understand things like zips, toilets or interest rates much better than we do. Researchers call this the illusion of explanatory depth: the feeling of understanding collapses the moment you have to spell out the mechanism step by step. Jargon is where the illusion hides, because a technical word can stand in for an explanation you don't actually have. Forcing yourself into plain words removes that hiding place, so the gaps become visible on the page.
parts.how:
1. Write the topic at the top of a blank page.
  2. Explain it, book closed, in simple sentences and short words, as if to a bright child. Use an analogy where you can.
  3. Mark every place where you hesitated, waved your hands or reached for a technical term.
  4. Go back to the source for exactly those spots, then rewrite the explanation.
  5. Read it aloud. If a sentence still sounds vague, simplify it once more.

examples.simple: Physics. "Why does a heavy ball and a light ball fall at the same speed?" You write "because gravity is the same" and stop: is the pull the same? No, the heavy ball is pulled harder, but it also needs a harder push to get moving. Those two cancel. That second sentence is the bit you didn't really have.
examples.nontrivial: Economics. Explaining "the central bank raises interest rates to fight inflation" in plain words forces a chain: borrowing gets dearer, people and firms borrow and spend less, shops can't raise prices as easily. You stall at "why would that lower prices rather than just slow growth?", which is exactly the debate economists have. A gap you found is often the most interesting part of the topic.

items.title: Learning by teaching
items.leadHtml: Teach a classmate, a study group, or even an empty room. Preparing to teach also helps.

parts.why: Two separate effects stack up. First, expecting to teach changes how you study: when students were told they would have to teach a passage (and then only took a test), they recalled more of it, organised it better and remembered the main points better than students who studied for a test. You start looking for structure, the "what matters and in what order", instead of collecting facts. This is sometimes called the protégé effect: we work harder for someone else's understanding than for our own. Second, actually explaining means retrieving from memory and building a connected story in real time, and a listener's "wait, why?" exposes gaps that silent reading never does.
parts.how:
1. Study the topic as if you have to give a 10-minute lesson on it tomorrow.
  2. Prepare a one-page outline: the 3-5 key ideas and one example each.
  3. Teach it without notes, to a friend, a study group, a parent, or aloud to an empty room or a voice recorder.
  4. Invite questions, or ask yourself the questions a confused learner would ask.
  5. Afterwards, write down every point where you stumbled and fix it from the source.

examples.simple: Languages. You explain to a friend when Spanish uses ser and when estar. Their question "then why is it está muerto, if being dead is permanent?" shows that your "permanent vs temporary" rule is too crude.
examples.nontrivial: Law. A study group splits a contract-law module: each person teaches one doctrine (offer and acceptance, consideration, misrepresentation) and brings two short problem cases. Preparing the cases forces you to find where the rule's edges are, and you learn the other doctrines through retrieval when you answer their questions.

  • Non-trivial: Law. A study group splits a contract-law module: each person teaches one doctrine (offer and acceptance, consideration, misrepresentation) and brings two short problem cases. Preparing the cases forces you to find where the rule's edges are, and you learn the other doctrines through retrieval when you answer their questions.

In the same time you could answer 40-80 recall questions. So reserve teaching for the core ideas that everything else hangs on, and use cheap recall for the rest.
parts.watch: Teaching without preparing turns into reading slides aloud, which is re-reading in disguise. And a polite audience that never asks questions gives you little; ask them to interrupt.

items.title: Dual coding
items.leadHtml: Pair words with visuals: diagrams, flowcharts, timelines, sketches. Redraw them from memory.

parts.why:
Memory stores verbal and visual information in partly separate ways. When an idea is held both as words and as a picture, you have two routes back to it, like a house with two doors: if one is locked, you can try the other. Drawing also forces decisions that text lets you skip, such as what comes first, what connects to what, and what is bigger.

Why it is not "learning styles". The claim that you learn best when teaching matches your preferred style ("I'm a visual learner") has not held up in well-designed tests. Dual coding is different: it says everyone benefits from combining words and meaningful visuals, and that the content decides the format. A map suits geography, a timeline suits history, and an argument is still best in words, whatever your preference.
parts.how:
1. Read a section, then close the book.
  2. Turn it into a visual: a flowchart for a process, a timeline for events, a labelled sketch for a structure, a graph for a relationship.
  3. Add short labels in words; the words and the picture should explain each other.
  4. A few days later, redraw it from a blank page and compare.

examples.simple: History. The causes of the First World War as a timeline with alliances drawn as lines between countries makes clear why one assassination pulled in so many states.
examples.nontrivial: Programming. Drawing what happens in memory when you copy a list in Python (two arrows to the same box vs two boxes) explains a bug that a page of text about "references" never quite does. The value comes from drawing it yourself and then checking it.
examples.html:
• Simple: History. The causes of the First World War as a timeline with alliances drawn as lines between countries makes clear why one assassination pulled in so many states.
  • Non-trivial: Programming. Drawing what happens in memory when you copy a list in Python (two arrows to the same box vs two boxes) explains a bug that a page of text about "references" never quite does. The value comes from drawing it yourself and then checking it.

parts.time: A quick sketch with labels takes about 5-10 min per paragraph, roughly 10-20× one recall question (rough estimates). Redrawing from memory later is the cheap, high-value part.
parts.watch: Decorative pictures and colour-coding don't count; the visual must carry meaning. Copying a textbook diagram neatly is mostly copying, so redraw it from memory instead.

items.title: Concrete examples
items.leadHtml: Link every abstract idea to a concrete case, example or story.

parts.why: Abstract ideas are hard to hold because there is nothing to grab. A concrete example hooks the new idea onto something you already know. But a single example has a hidden cost: you can't tell which of its features matter. Learn "opportunity cost" only from "the cinema ticket instead of the concert" and you may think it is about money or leisure. With two or three examples that look different on the surface but share the same structure, your brain is pushed to extract what they have in common, which is the concept itself. That is why several varied examples beat one.
parts.how:
1. For each abstract idea, find one example in your source.
  2. Find or invent a second (and ideally a third) from a different context.
  3. Say what the examples share and what is irrelevant about each.
  4. Test yourself the other way round: given a new case, decide whether it is an example of the idea, and why.

examples.simple: Biology. "Negative feedback" = a thermostat switching the heating off when the room is warm enough. Second example: blood sugar rises, insulin is released, blood sugar falls. Now "the output turns down its own cause" is clear, and it is not about heating.
examples.nontrivial: Economics and law. "Moral hazard": a person who drives less carefully after buying full car insurance; a bank that takes bigger risks because it expects a bailout; a tenant who doesn't care for a flat when the deposit is small. Three very different surfaces, one structure: someone protected from the cost of their behaviour takes more risk. A good check is a near-miss: someone who buys insurance because they already drive badly is a different idea (adverse selection).

parts.watch: Examples that are too similar teach the surface, not the idea. And check invented examples against the source; a wrong example teaches the wrong concept.

items.title: Pretesting (errorful generation)
items.leadHtml: Try questions on a topic before you study it. Getting them wrong primes you to notice the answers.

parts.why: It sounds backwards: how can a test on something you haven't learned help? A failed attempt does two things. It opens a "slot" in your mind, a question you now care about, so when the answer arrives you notice it and it sticks. And your wrong guess activates related knowledge, so the right answer links to more of what you already know. It is like being told a riddle before hearing the punchline: the punchline lands. Experiments find that people who first guess and get it wrong often remember the material better than people who spent the same time just studying it, as long as they see the correct answer soon after.
parts.how:
1. Before a lecture, chapter or video, take 2-3 questions (from the end of the chapter, the learning objectives, a past paper, or your own guesses at what will be asked).
  2. Answer each one in a few seconds. Guess freely; being wrong is the point.
  3. Then study the material and look out for the answers.
  4. Afterwards, check your guesses against the correct answers.

examples.simple: Languages. Before a lesson on German noun genders, guess the gender of Mädchen (girl). You will likely say feminine; it is neuter (das Mädchen), because every word ending in -chen is neuter. That surprise anchors the rule.
examples.nontrivial: Medicine and statistics. Before a lecture on diagnostic tests, ask: "A test is 99% accurate and the disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. You test positive. How likely is it you have it?" Most people guess about 99%; the answer is about 9%. Having been wrong, you will follow the lecture's explanation of base rates closely, and you won't forget it.

  • Non-trivial: Medicine and statistics. Before a lecture on diagnostic tests, ask: "A test is 99% accurate and the disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. You test positive. How likely is it you have it?" Most people guess about 99%; the answer is about 9%. Having been wrong, you will follow the lecture's explanation of base rates closely, and you won't forget it.

items.bodyHtml:
Try questions on a topic before you study it. Getting them wrong primes you to notice the answers.

Why it works. It sounds backwards: how can a test on something you haven't learned help? A failed attempt does two things. It opens a "slot" in your mind, a question you now care about, so when the answer arrives you notice it and it sticks. And your wrong guess activates related knowledge, so the right answer links to more of what you already know. It is like being told a riddle before hearing the punchline: the punchline lands. Experiments find that people who first guess and get it wrong often remember the material better than people who spent the same time just studying it, as long as they see the correct answer soon after.

How to do it.

  1. Before a lecture, chapter or video, take 2-3 questions (from the end of the chapter, the learning objectives, a past paper, or your own guesses at what will be asked).
  2. Answer each one in a few seconds. Guess freely; being wrong is the point.
  3. Then study the material and look out for the answers.
  4. Afterwards, check your guesses against the correct answers.

Examples.

  • Simple: Languages. Before a lesson on German noun genders, guess the gender of Mädchen (girl). You will likely say feminine; it is neuter (das Mädchen), because every word ending in -chen is neuter. That surprise anchors the rule.
  • Non-trivial: Medicine and statistics. Before a lecture on diagnostic tests, ask: "A test is 99% accurate and the disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. You test positive. How likely is it you have it?" Most people guess about 99%; the answer is about 9%. Having been wrong, you will follow the lecture's explanation of base rates closely, and you won't forget it.

⏱ Time cost. 2-3 questions before reading take about 1-2 min per paragraph, roughly 2-4× one recall question (rough estimates). One of the cheapest techniques here.

Watch out. The benefit depends on getting the correct answer soon afterwards; a wrong guess that is never corrected can stick. Keep it short and low-stakes, and don't let it replace testing after study.

items.title: Successive relearning
items.leadHtml: Keep retrieving each item until you get it right, then come back on later days and do it again.

parts.why: It joins the two strongest techniques into one routine. Within a session you keep testing each item until you can produce it correctly (retrieval to a criterion), so nothing is left half-learned. Across sessions, spacing lets the memory fade a little, so each relearning takes effort and makes it stronger. A useful picture is a path through a field: walking it once leaves a trace that grows over; walking it again every few days, each time a bit more overgrown, turns it into a path that lasts. Relearning also gets faster each time, so the later sessions cost little. In classroom studies, students who used it remembered substantially more on course exams and weeks later.
parts.how:
1. Turn the material into questions or flashcards.
  2. Session 1: go through them; anything you miss goes back into the pile until you answer it correctly once (some people use twice).
  3. Come back after a gap, for example 2 days, then a week, then 2-3 weeks.
  4. In each later session, again keep retrieving until each item is correct once.
  5. Drop items that are quick and correct on the first try in two sessions running; keep the slow or missed ones.

examples.simple: Music. Learning the order of sharps for key signatures (F, C, G, D, A, E, B): recall it until correct today, then again on Thursday and next Monday. By the third session it takes seconds.
examples.nontrivial: Maths. A list of 15 trigonometric identities and integration rules for an exam. In session 1 you need several rounds for some of them; by session 3 you get most right first time, and the ones that still fail tell you which rules you don't understand (not just haven't memorised), which is where to go back to the derivation.

items.title: A simple rule of thumb
items.leadHtml:
Spend less time taking information in and more time getting it back out. A good target is at least half of study time spent on retrieval (questions, recall, cards) rather than reading or watching.

The reason is in the time-cost numbers above: one minute of retrieval usually buys more lasting memory than one minute of reading, and a session that is all input feels productive but leaves little behind a week later. Input is still needed; you can't recall what you never took in. The point is the balance.

Here is what that can look like in a 2-hour session on one new topic (say, a chapter on the French Revolution, a lecture on enzymes, or a unit on recursion):

TimeActivityType
0:00-0:05Due flashcard reviews from earlier topicsRetrieval
0:05-0:10Pretest: 3 questions on today's chapter, guessingRetrieval
0:10-0:40Read or watch the new material once, with the pretest questions in mindInput
0:40-0:55Blank-page recall of what you just read, then check and fill gaps in another colourRetrieval
0:55-1:05BreakRest
1:05-1:20Clarify the gaps from the source; sketch one diagram or find two examples for the hardest ideaInput and elaboration
1:20-1:45Practice questions mixing today's topic with last week's; read the explanation for every missRetrieval
1:45-1:55Explain the one central idea aloud in plain words (a short Feynman pass)Retrieval
1:55-2:00Make 5-10 flashcards for facts you missed, to come back in successive relearningPlanning

That is about 60 minutes of retrieval against 45 of input and elaboration, a little over half of the 110 working minutes. Notice where the expensive techniques go: one diagram, two examples and one plain-words explanation, all spent on the central idea, while the cheap techniques (cards, recall, questions) carry the rest.
